title: A book or the book?
goal: Master the object suffix *-ыг / -ийг*: the one place where Mongolian marks the difference English marks with *a* and *the*.
bekal: add the object suffix only when it's needed, and know when it isn't
build sentences with two objects at once without getting lost

dialogs.title: Яриа — Номын санд
dialogs.intro: Budi is looking for a book in the university library. The librarian helps him.

notes: ⚠️ **This is the heart of the unit: compare the first and third lines.** *Би **ном** хайж байна* = "I'm looking for a book" (any book, not one I have in mind). *Би **номыг** хайж байна* = "I'm looking for **the** book" (a specific book we've already talked about). The object suffix is how Mongolian says "the."

**Түүнийг = "that/him/her" in object form.** Pronouns have their own object forms: *би* → *намайг*, *чи* → *чамайг*, *та* → *таныг*, *тэр* → *түүнийг*. They're irregular and must be memorized, because they're used constantly.

**Толь бичиг literally means "mirror writing" and is the word for dictionary.** Mongolian loves images like this: *гар утас* (hand phone) for a mobile phone, *галт тэрэг* (fire cart) for a train, *нисдэг тэрэг* (flying cart) for a helicopter. When you meet a strange compound, translate its parts; the meaning is usually obvious.

**Байвал and хэтэрвэл carry the suffix -вал / -вэл, meaning "if."** *Асуулт **байвал*** = "if there are questions." This suffix attaches to verbs and is very common; it's covered fully at A2, but learn to recognize it now.

⚠️ **Look at the word order in the last line of the dialogue: *Та надад маш их тусаллаа*.** The recipient (*надад*, to me) stands **before** the verb, like everything else. Mongolian never puts anything after the verb.

grammars.title: When the object takes a suffix, and when it doesn't
body: This is the only part of Mongolian grammar that truly demands a decision every time you speak. Luckily, the rule boils down to one question: **does the listener know which thing I mean?**

head: Use the suffix if…
Example
Meaning
rows: The thing is **a person or a name**
The object is **far** from its verb

after: **And don't use the suffix when the thing is indefinite, general, or fused with the verb.** *Би ном уншина* (I read books, the activity of reading); *би хоол иднэ* (I eat, the activity of eating); *би монгол хэл сурна* (I study Mongolian).

⚠️ **English speakers' most common mistake is overusing the suffix**, because "the" is everywhere in English and it feels natural to mark every object you'd say "the" with. Mongolian is stingier: **when in doubt, leave it off.** An object without the suffix sounds neutral; a wrongly suffixed object sounds as if you're pointing at something the listener doesn't know.

grammars.title: Forms of the object suffix
body: Three forms, chosen by the word's last letter and its vowel group: exactly the same pattern as the possessive suffix in unit 2.
after: Pronouns have their own forms to memorize: *намайг* (me), *чамайг* (you, informal), *таныг* (you, formal), *түүнийг* (him/her/that), *биднийг* (us), *тэднийг* (them), *энийг* (this), *тэрийг* (that).

**One exercise that really helps:** take ten sentences from the unit 6 dialogue and ask of each object: "Does the listener know which thing I mean?" If yes, add the suffix. If not, leave it bare. Do it once and the rule sticks.

head: Subject
Object
Say it
Example
rows: *Би чамайг хүлээнэ.* — I'll wait for you.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice that *тэр* has **two** object forms: *түүнийг* when it means "him/her," and *тэрийг* when it means "that" (a thing). This is the only place Mongolian separates people from things, and even here it's optional: in casual speech people often use *түүнийг* for both.

blocks.title: Verbs that almost always take a suffixed object
items: *дуудах* (to call), *хүлээх* (to wait for), *таних* (to know a person), *урих* (to invite), *харах* (to see someone): they all target **a specific person**, so their object is almost always suffixed.
Compare: *хоол хийх* (to cook), *ном унших* (to read), *хэл сурах* (to study a language): all general activities, so their object is almost always bare.
⚠️ This isn't a grammar rule but a consequence of meaning. People are always specific; general activities aren't.

blocks.text: Verbs like *өгөх* (to give), *хэлэх* (to tell), and *үзүүлэх* (to show) need two targets: the thing and the person. Mongolian marks them with different suffixes, so their order can be swapped without changing the meaning.

head: Sentence
Meaning
Note
rows: The teacher teaches the lesson to the students.
Both roles are clear from the suffixes.
The book, I gave to him.
The object moves to the front for emphasis.

blocks.text: The last row shows a big advantage of the suffix system: **because every word's role is marked, the order can change for emphasis.** English has to use a passive or a clumsy fronting ("That book, I gave to him…"). Mongolian just moves the word to the front.

sections.title: Verbs that pair with an object

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Туслах* (to help) takes the suffix **-д**, not the object suffix: you "help **to** someone." *Надад тусалсан*, not *намайг тусалсан*. There are a few verbs like this, and it's best to memorize them with their suffix, just as you learn "depend **on**" and not "depend of" in English.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the object suffix -ыг, -ийг, or -г. If no suffix is needed, write a dash.
Change the pronoun into its object form.
Put the words in the right order.
